chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim narrated from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from al-Hasan ibn Atiyyah, from Umar ibn Yazid, who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'A man sends me al-bukhtaj (a type of drink) from among our non-Shia companions.' He said: 'If he is among those who consider the intoxicant permissible, do not drink it; and if he is among those who do not consider it permissible, then drink it.'

key_terms.اَلْبُخْتَجَ: A specific type of drink, often identified as wine or a fermented beverage.

ai.seo_question: How do Shia jurists determine the permissibility of drinking gifts from non-Shia based on their view of intoxicants?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* illustrates the Shia principle of *al-istihlal* (theological conviction) determining the purity of gifts from non-Shia, where the giver's belief in the permissibility of wine renders the drink impure (*najis*) even if physically clean. It highlights the juristic distinction between mere consumption of alcohol and the doctrinal acceptance of its legality, a key nuance in Shia fiqh regarding external purity. This reflects the broader Shia emphasis on the spiritual and theological status of the giver influencing the ritual purity of the gift.
